name: Times club monthly special crossword No 289

solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Equipment cuts narrow openings, twisting curved old blades

indicators.note: to twist something round is to turn it the other way, so these letters run backwards
a thing that cuts into another sits inside it, splitting it in two

blocks.note: slits are long narrow openings
a rig is a set of equipment, as in a drilling rig

explanation.surface: A workshop where some equipment slices thin slits in old curved blades.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Equipment' sits at the start like a definition, but the definition is at the far end; the openings are turned round and then split open by the equipment.
explanation.definitionFit: A strigil was a curved metal scraper Romans and Greeks used to clean sweat and oil from the skin.

clue.text: Stale beer at first treated as poor “wallop”?

indicators.note: what comes at first is the opening of each word, so only initials are kept

blocks.note: the initials of three words
to wallop someone is to strike them hard, to lash them

explanation.surface: Flat beer is served up as poor-quality wallop, slang for beer.
explanation.walkthrough: Wallop is British slang for beer, hence the quotation marks and question mark: here it means a blow. The initials of 'treated as poor' come first.
explanation.definitionFit: Taplash is an old word for weak or dregs-quality beer, the last poor drawings from a cask.

clue.text: Half of pictures with bloke dominated by missus that’s incredible

indicators.note: taking only half means the other half of the word is thrown away
in a down answer, a thing dominated by another sits beneath it, so the second piece comes first

blocks.note: images are pictures; its first half is kept
my old Dutch is Cockney slang for a wife
a bloke is a man

explanation.surface: Half the photos show a henpecked bloke bossed by his wife, which is hard to believe.
explanation.walkthrough: Dutch, short for duchess (of Fife), is Cockney rhyming slang for wife. The missus sits above the bloke in the down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a British idiom of disbelief, as in 'if that is true, then I am a Dutchman'.

clue.text: Thessalian king exposed bribery over charges

indicators.note: something exposed has had its covering stripped off, so the outer letters go

blocks.note: a fix is a bribe or rigging arrangement
ions are electrically charged particles

explanation.surface: An ancient ruler is unmasked for taking bribes in exchange for dropping charges.
explanation.walkthrough: FIX and IONS are joined to make FIXIONS, and the whole thing then loses its first and last letters to give IXION.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth Ixion ruled the Lapiths of Thessaly and was bound to a fiery wheel for courting Hera.

clue.text: Two fifths of scrap iron initially picked up taking away waste metal

indicators.note: a word of five letters cut to two fifths keeps its opening pair and loses the other three
initially means at the very start, so only the opening letter is wanted
in a down entry, picking something up lifts it so it reads from the bottom upwards

blocks.note: taken as written, then cut to its first two letters
first letter
less means minus, taking away

explanation.surface: Someone picks up bits of scrap iron while clearing away waste metal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Picked up' looks like collecting scrap, but it turns LESS upside down in the column. 'Scrap iron' looks like the definition, yet it only supplies letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Scissel is the metal clippings or the strip left over after blanks for coins are punched out.

clue.text: Eastern condiment that double helping of medicinal plant would contain

indicators.note: the answer is what the longer string would contain, so the letters around it are dropped

blocks.note: balsam is a medicinal plant; written out twice, a run of six letters straddles the join

explanation.surface: A spicy Asian sauce that would be packed with a herbal remedy taken twice.
explanation.walkthrough: The plant's letters are not in the clue, so this is not an ordinary hidden word: write BALSAM twice and the answer sits inside, balSAMBALsam.
explanation.definitionFit: Sambal is a hot chilli relish from Indonesia and Malaysia, served as a side condiment.

clue.text: Gun operator starts to aim into channel with a narrow opening

indicators.note: the starts of words are their first letters, so only initials are kept

blocks.note: the Sten is a British submachine gun
OP is short for operator
initials of three words

explanation.surface: A gunner begins to take aim through a slot of a channel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Into' looks like a container signal, but it is just one of three words whose initials are taken.
explanation.definitionFit: Stenopaic describes something, such as spectacles for the eye, fitted with a tiny slit or pinhole.

clue.text: Former unit deserted by front, as this observer sees it

indicators.note: when the front deserts, the leading letter walks away and is lost

blocks.note: the internet abbreviation for 'in my humble opinion'

explanation.surface: A one-time army unit is abandoned by the front line, in the narrator's view.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unit' suggests a military unit and 'front' a battlefront, but the unit is one of measurement, and the front is just a first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The mho was the old unit of electrical conductance, ohm spelt backwards, now replaced by the siemens.

clue.text: Clovers the same in appearance around southern tip of Spain

indicators.note: one thing placed around another encloses it
a tip is an end point, here the first letter of the word

blocks.note: things alike look the same
S is the abbreviation for southern
first letter

explanation.surface: Clover plants look identical all around the southern tip of Spain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Southern tip of Spain' reads as one place, but it splits: 'southern' goes inside the look-alike word, and the tip of Spain is simply its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Alsike is a species of clover grown for fodder, named after a village in Sweden.

clue.text: Failure points condemned ductile metal bearing

indicators.note: a condemned building is wrecked, so these letters are knocked down and rebuilt

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An engineer's report damns the weak spots in a soft metal bearing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bearing' looks like the machine part a metal bearing would be; here it means carrying, the adjective ending of the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Platinum is a soft, ductile metal, and rock described this way contains or yields platinum ore.

clue.text: Mostly optimistic when delivering first new monkey

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the final letter is cut
to deliver something is to hand it over, so the first such letter is given up

blocks.note: a sanguine person is hopeful and optimistic
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A hopeful new monkey, hailed as it is delivered at a zoo.
explanation.walkthrough: SANGUINE loses its last letter, then gives up the first of its two Ns; 'delivering' sounds like a birth, but it means handing over.
explanation.definitionFit: Saguin is another name for the marmoset, a small South American primate also spelt sagoin.

clue.text: Acceptable training clothes on cool Canadian lounger?

definitions.note: the question mark flags 'lounger' as a loose name for a slow, idle person

indicators.note: to clothe something is to wrap it up, so one piece dresses another
one piece placed on another follows straight after it in an across answer

blocks.note: to cool down, as of an economy, is to slow
PE is physical education, school sports training
OK means acceptable

explanation.surface: Decent gym clothes worn by a laid-back Canadian lying on a sun lounger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clothes' looks like a noun, gym kit, but it is a verb: PE clothes OK. 'Cool' is a verb too, as in cool off.
explanation.definitionFit: Slowpoke is North American slang for a dawdler, someone who idles about, as Canadians would say.

clue.text: Evolutionary theory criticises 60 per cent of sexually liberated maidens

indicators.note: keeping six tenths of a ten-letter word throws away its last four

blocks.note: to pan is to review harshly
a permissive society is sexually liberated
M is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for maiden overs

explanation.surface: A theory of evolution attacks most free-loving young women.
explanation.walkthrough: A maiden in cricket is an over with no runs scored, recorded as M. 'Maidens' and 'sexually liberated' make a racy picture that hides the cricket.
explanation.definitionFit: Panspermism holds that life's seeds are spread through the universe and began life on Earth, an origin theory.

clue.text: Lizard seen in ditch area bordering rampart

indicators.note: a thing bordering another lies right beside it, so the two pieces sit side by side

blocks.note: to ditch something is to chuck it away
a rampart is a defensive wall
A is the abbreviation for area

explanation.surface: A lizard spotted in a trench beside a fortress wall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ditch' looks like the trench of the picture, but it is the verb meaning throw away.
explanation.definitionFit: The chuckwalla is a large iguana of the deserts of the southwestern United States and Mexico.

clue.text: In literature, anything that he wrote was unopened, sadly

indicators.note: a thing left unopened has not had its front broken, here meaning the first letter is gone
things that go sadly go badly wrong, so these letters end up out of order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, then losing its first letter

explanation.surface: Anything the writer ever wrote went unread, more's the pity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In literature' marks the answer as a poetic contraction, the kind found in old verse, and belongs to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Whatsoe'er is the poetic shortened form of whatsoever, meaning anything at all.

clue.text: North Sea Gas light progressively shows yellow for locals

indicators.note: moving on step by step, one letter further into each successive word

blocks.note: first letter
second letter
third letter
fourth letter

explanation.surface: A gas flare in the North Sea burns with a yellow light visible to people living nearby.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yellow' looks like the colour of the flame, but it means cowardly, and 'for locals' marks a dialect word.
explanation.definitionFit: Nesh is northern English dialect for soft, feeble or timid, and so cowardly, also used of feeling the cold.

clue.text: Scots daydream of whiskey loco going round Borders

indicators.note: something going round turns about and so faces the other way
to border something is to run along its edges, enclosing it

blocks.note: loco is slang for crazy, mad
Whiskey is W in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A Scotsman's whisky-fuelled dream of a steam engine chugging round the Scottish Borders.
explanation.walkthrough: The Borders is a region of Scotland, which fits the picture, but here 'Borders' is a verb, and 'loco' is not a locomotive.
explanation.definitionFit: Dwam is Scots for a stupor or swoon, a dreamy state of mind where one is lost in thought.

clue.text: Slender racer gets extra “line” twice and “blow” once

indicators.note: adding one stroke to a letter shape turns it into another letter, done here two times

blocks.note: a whippet is a slim racing dog

explanation.surface: A thin racing dog is given more lead twice and a blow once.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'line' is a pen stroke: draw a diagonal leg on the bowl of a P and it becomes an R. Do that to both Ps of WHIPPET.
explanation.definitionFit: Whirret is an obsolete word for a smart blow or box on the ear, hence 'once', meaning formerly.

clue.text: Body in blood found in uncovered skip by staff, reportedly

indicators.note: something uncovered has had its outer layer removed, so the ends go
what is reported is passed on by word of mouth, so this is how it is said

blocks.note: to gambol is to skip and frolic
a sceptre is a ceremonial staff

explanation.surface: A corpse in a pool of blood is discovered in an open skip, according to staff.
explanation.walkthrough: A skip is a British open-topped rubbish container, which drives the murder picture; here it is the verb to leap. 'Body' is a biological body, not a corpse.
explanation.definitionFit: An amboceptor is an antibody in blood serum that links an antigen to complement, so it is a body in blood.

clue.text: Mistake about including rampant misery in epic poem

indicators.note: turned about means facing the other direction
rampant means running wild and unchecked, so these letters are out of control
to include something is to take it inside

blocks.note: a flub is a blunder
woe is misery

explanation.surface: A critic objects to rampant misery being included in an epic poem.
explanation.walkthrough: FLUB turned round is BULF, and the jumbled misery goes in after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Beowulf is the Old English epic poem about a hero who slays the monster Grendel and later a dragon.

clue.text: Blood serum component’s old ID code cracked by boy

indicators.note: whatever cracks a thing breaks open into it and ends up lodged inside

blocks.note: O is the abbreviation for old
a PIN is a personal identification number
a son is a boy

explanation.surface: A young lad cracks the old password protecting a blood test result.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s is 'is', linking definition to wordplay rather than a possessive.
explanation.definitionFit: An opsonin is an antibody in blood serum that coats bacteria so white cells can engulf them.

clue.text: Son boards deck on liner amidships wearing excellent boots

indicators.note: one who boards gets on first, so this piece is placed before the next
amidships is the middle of a vessel, so the centre letter is taken
something wearing a garment is inside it

blocks.note: fine means excellent
middle letter
S is the abbreviation for son
to deck someone is to knock them out, KO

explanation.surface: A son walks on deck aboard a cruise liner wearing excellent boots.
explanation.walkthrough: The ship words all mislead: 'deck' means floor someone, 'boards' places the son ahead of it, and only 'amidships' is used nautically, for the centre letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Finnesko are Lapp boots of reindeer skin with the fur outside, worn by polar explorers.

clue.text: Closer to identifying unknown flower marked with wavy lines

indicators.note: the closer of a word is what finishes it, its final letter

blocks.note: last letter
Y is an unknown quantity in algebra
the rose is a flower

explanation.surface: A botanist gets closer to naming a mystery bloom with wavy markings.
explanation.walkthrough: In algebra the unknowns are X, Y and Z, so 'unknown' supplies one of them.
explanation.definitionFit: Gyrose is a botanical term for surfaces bearing wavy or folded ridges, like some fungus caps.

clue.text: Wan celeb covering Maori village folk dance

indicators.note: a thing covering another goes around it

blocks.note: Gok Wan is a British TV stylist and presenter
a pa is a fortified Maori village

explanation.surface: A pale celebrity hides a Maori village behind a folk dance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wan' looks like the adjective for pale, but it is a surname: Gok Wan presents fashion makeover shows on British television.
explanation.definitionFit: The gopak, or hopak, is an energetic Ukrainian folk dance with high leaps, danced by men.

clue.text: Droll member beginning to upset another actively into common sense

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its first letter, the only one kept
acting actively means moving about, so these letters are set in motion

blocks.note: rum is old British slang for odd or droll
a leg is a limb, a member of the body
first letter
another member, this time a Member of Parliament
taken as written

explanation.surface: A funny politician starts to rile a rival into seeing sense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Another' leans on the previous word: having had one member, a limb, you take another member, an MP. 'Into' is fodder, not a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Rumlegumption is a Scots variant of rumgumption, meaning shrewd practical wisdom or gumption.

clue.text: Run away from goal to induce Glaswegian?

definitions.note: an infinitive phrase for the verb, flagged as Scots

indicators.note: when a run, R in cricket, leaves the word it is no longer there

blocks.note: a mark is a target or goal

explanation.surface: A footballer runs off the goal line to tempt a Glasgow striker.
explanation.walkthrough: R stands for run in cricket scoring. The question mark warns that the Glaswegian is not a person but the language the answer is in.
explanation.definitionFit: Mak is the Scots form of make, and to make someone do something is to induce them.

clue.text: Puff on joint blocks senior Irish author

indicators.note: something that blocks a passage sits in the middle of it

blocks.note: SR is the abbreviation for senior
a toke is a drag on a cannabis cigarette

explanation.surface: A drag on a spliff holds up an elderly Irish writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Joint' and 'blocks' could be carpentry, but the joint is a cannabis cigarette.
explanation.definitionFit: Bram Stoker was the Dublin-born novelist who wrote Dracula in 1897.

clue.text: Periodically keep subordinates probing gross swindle

indicators.note: periodically means at regular intervals, so every other letter is kept
a probe pushes into something, so these letters go inside

blocks.note: gross means obese, fat
alternate letters
men are the junior ranks under an officer

explanation.surface: A boss regularly keeps underlings investigating a large-scale fraud.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gross' suggests gross fraud or the total amount, but it is the adjective for fat.
explanation.definitionFit: Fakement is old slang for a dodge, trick or counterfeit, the work of a swindler.
